lead: This unit teaches how to design Python programs with classes and objects. It moves from a first class with attributes and methods to inheritance, polymorphism, abstract classes, iterators, generators and decorators. After it, a student can model a small real system, reuse code safely and explain method lookup and object lifetime.
about: Unit 4 builds object-oriented Python in eight steps. Chapter 4.1 defines classes, objects, attributes and methods. Chapter 4.2 adds constructors, destructors and the self keyword to control object lifetime. Chapter 4.3 hides state behind encapsulation and abstraction using accessors and mutators. Chapter 4.4 extends classes by single, multiple and hierarchical inheritance with super(). Chapter 4.5 explains overriding and the method resolution order, a topic only a few universities teach. Chapter 4.6 covers polymorphism, operator overloading and duck typing. Chapter 4.7 turns shared behaviour into abstract classes and interface-like base classes. Chapter 4.8 closes with iterators, generators and decorators, which make objects and functions work in loops and wrappers. Each chapter assumes the earlier one and leaves basic syntax to Units 1 and 2.

chapters.idea: A class packages data attributes and behaviour methods, and each object has its own state.
chapters.depth: Define class and object; class attributes versus instance attributes; method definition with self; creating two objects; calling methods; __str__ preview; rules for a simple class (name, docstring, attributes, methods). Some syllabi call this the blueprint/instance relationship. Mention __init__ only as object setup; full constructor work comes in 4.2.

figure.title: Class to objects
figure.aria: A class BankAccount with class attribute bank_name SBI is the blueprint for two objects, Asha with balance 6500 and Ravi with balance 1200.

chapters.example: Create BankAccount with class attribute bank_name='SBI'. Its __init__ sets holder and balance. Make a1=BankAccount('Asha',5000) and a2=BankAccount('Ravi',1200). Call a1.deposit(1500). Print a1.balance, a2.balance and a1.bank_name.
chapters.trap: Writing def deposit(amount) without self, so Python raises TypeError or sets a local variable; every instance method needs self as its first parameter.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 variables and data types; Unit 2 functions and parameters.
chapters.leave: Constructor and destructor details to 4.2; access control to 4.3; inheritance to 4.4.

chapters.idea: __init__ initialises each new object, __del__ runs near object destruction, and self binds a method to its instance.
chapters.depth: __init__ as initializer/constructor, parameters and default values, self binding, __del__ as destructor, object lifetime (creation, use, deletion), reference counting and garbage-collection timing, del obj versus __del__, and the rule that __init__ returns None. Name __new__ briefly only. Some syllabi call __init__ the initializer.

figure.title: Object lifetime
figure.aria: Creating c1 calls __init__ and sets count to 1; creating c2 sets count to 2; del c1 calls __del__, lowers count to 1 and the final print shows 1.

chapters.example: Define class Counter with class variable count=0. __init__(self,n) sets self.n=n and adds 1 to Counter.count. __del__(self) subtracts 1 and prints 'bye', self.n. Write c1=Counter(5); c2=Counter(7); print(Counter.count); del c1; print(Counter.count). Give the output.
chapters.trap: Treating __del__ as guaranteed cleanup: its timing is not fixed, it may run at interpreter shutdown, and it is unsafe for closing files.
chapters.leave: with and file closing to Unit 5; memory allocator details outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Encapsulation hides internal state behind methods, and abstraction exposes only the safe interface.
chapters.depth: Encapsulation and data hiding: public names, _protected convention, __private name mangling; accessors (getters) and mutators (setters); validation; @property read and write basics; abstraction as showing what a method does, not how. Some syllabi call mutators setters. Show that double underscore is name mangling, not a security lock.

figure.title: Validated setter
figure.aria: A client calls set_celsius(25), which passes the -273.15 check and stores 25; set_celsius(-300) fails, raises ValueError, and the stored 25 stays.

chapters.example: Define Temperature with private __celsius=0. set_celsius validates value >= -273.15 and stores it; get_celsius returns it. Create t, call t.set_celsius(25), print t.get_celsius(); call t.set_celsius(-300), catch ValueError and print t.get_celsius().
chapters.trap: Assuming __celsius is impossible to access; Python only renames it to _Temperature__celsius, and direct assignment t.__celsius=-300 creates a new attribute, bypassing validation.
chapters.leave: Abstract interfaces to 4.7; exception handling details to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A subclass reuses a parent class, and super() calls the next class in the method resolution order.
chapters.depth: Base and derived classes; single inheritance; hierarchical inheritance (one base, many children); multiple inheritance syntax class C(A,B); multilevel inheritance briefly; super() for constructor chaining; isinstance and issubclass. Mention cooperative super in multiple inheritance, but leave full C3 order to 4.5.

figure.aria: Person is the base class; Student with roll 23 and Teacher with subject Python are two child classes in a hierarchical inheritance tree.

chapters.example: Define Person with __init__(name) storing name. Define Student(Person) with __init__(name, roll) calling super().__init__(name). Define Teacher(Person) with __init__(name, subject) calling super().__init__(name). Create s=Student('Ravi',23), t=Teacher('Meera','Python'); print s.name, s.roll, t.name, t.subject.
chapters.trap: Forgetting super().__init__(...) so the parent part is never initialised; in multiple inheritance super() does not mean 'call every parent'.
chapters.leave: Overriding and C3 MRO to 4.5; abstract base classes to 4.7.

chapters.idea: A subclass method can replace a parent method, and Python finds methods by walking the class's method resolution order.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic in detail. Cover overriding, calling the parent version with super(), __mro__, the idea of C3 linearization, the diamond problem and cooperative constructors. Keep to reading an MRO and predicting output; do not prove the C3 algorithm.

figure.aria: Diamond inheritance with D inheriting B and C, both inheriting A; the MRO of D is D, B, C, A.

chapters.example: Classes A, B(A), C(A) and D(B,C) each append their class name to self.order and call super().__init__(). D first creates self.order and appends 'D'. Create D() and print d.order.
chapters.trap: Assuming super() calls only the direct parent; in a diamond it calls the next class in the MRO, so A runs once after C, not twice.
chapters.leave: Full C3 proof and metaclasses outside this unit; abstract classes to 4.7.

chapters.idea: The same operation can work on different types because Python chooses behaviour from the object's methods at runtime.
chapters.depth: Polymorphism by overriding; operator overloading for __add__, __sub__, __mul__, __eq__, __lt__, __str__ and __len__; comparison methods and equality; duck typing (method presence, not type names); functions as first-class objects; map, filter, reduce, lambda and jump tables via dictionaries of functions, linked briefly to Unit 2. Some syllabi call this dynamic polymorphism.

figure.title: Money addition
figure.aria: Two Money objects, 10 rupees 50 paise and 5 rupees 25 paise, go through the __add__ method and produce a new Money object of 15 rupees 75 paise.

chapters.example: Define Money with rupees and paise, normalise paise >=100, __add__ returns a new Money, __eq__ compares total paise, and __str__ prints like ₹15.75. Take m1=Money(10,50), m2=Money(5,25), m3=Money(10,50). Print m1+m2, m1==m3, m1==m2.
chapters.trap: Thinking polymorphism needs a common base class; duck typing works from method names alone, so a missing method is caught only when it is called.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 to 4.4; Unit 2 lambda, map, filter and reduce.
chapters.leave: Full map/filter/reduce practice to Unit 2; abstract interfaces to 4.7.

chapters.idea: An abstract base class defines a required interface and cannot be instantiated until subclasses implement its abstract methods.
chapters.depth: abc.ABC and @abstractmethod; instantiation failure; subclasses must implement every abstract method; abstract properties; interface-like pure abstract classes; Python has no interface keyword, so ABC and multiple inheritance provide contracts. Some syllabi call these interfaces.

figure.aria: Abstract Shape is the parent; Circle with radius 2 and Rectangle with sides 3 and 4 implement its abstract area method.

chapters.example: Define abstract Shape with abstract area(). Circle(radius) implements area as πr²; Rectangle(w,h) implements w*h. Create Circle(2) and Rectangle(3,4); print their areas using π=3.1416; then try Shape().
chapters.trap: Expecting ABC alone to block instantiation; the class needs at least one @abstractmethod, and a subclass that misses one stays abstract.
chapters.leave: Java-style interface syntax to other languages; decorator mechanics to 4.8.

chapters.idea: Iterators produce items one at a time, generators create iterators with yield, and decorators wrap functions or classes to add behaviour.
chapters.depth: Iterable versus iterator; __iter__ and __next__; StopIteration; the for-loop protocol; generator functions with yield, lazy evaluation and generator expressions; decorators as higher-order functions, @syntax, wrapper functions, functools.wraps, and decorating methods; mention class decorators. Some syllabi call generators resumable functions.

figure.aria: The caller asks generator g for values in order: next gives 1, next gives 4, list gives 9 and 16, and the second list gives an empty list.

chapters.example: Write generator squares(n) that yields i*i for i in 1..n. Set g=squares(4). Print next(g), next(g), list(g), then list(g) again. Give the output.
chapters.trap: Trying to reuse a generator after it is exhausted; it is a one-pass iterator, so a second list(g) returns [].
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 functions; 4.1 instance methods; 4.7 for @abstractmethod as a decorator.
chapters.leave: Async generators and context managers outside this unit; file iteration to Unit 5.

links: self holds hidden state for safe access
polymorphism is fixed by abstract interfaces
